blocks.explanation:
\({}^{5}C_{3}\) is the number of ways to choose 3 things out of 5 different things when order does not matter.
We must find its value.
Plan: use \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\), cancel the bigger factorial, then multiply and divide.
steps:
Given: \(n = 5\), \(r = 3\).
To find: \({}^{5}C_{3}\).
Method: \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\). It is the permutation \({}^{n}P_{r}\) divided by \(r!\), because each group of \(r\) things can be put in order in \(r!\) ways.

Cancel \(3!\) and calculate
\[= \dfrac{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3!}{3! \cdot 2 \cdot 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{5 \cdot 4}{2} = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\]
Why: \(5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3!\). Writing \(5!\) only down to the bigger factorial at the bottom (\(3!\)) lets it cancel at once.

Check with Pascal's rule
\[{}^{4}C_{3} + {}^{4}C_{2} = 4 + 6\]
\[= 10 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Pascal's rule \({}^{n}C_{r} + {}^{n}C_{r-1} = {}^{n+1}C_{r}\) (proved in Question 14) gives the same value from smaller combinations.

blocks.explanation:
\({}^{8}C_{5}\) is the number of ways to choose 5 things out of 8 different things when order does not matter.
We must find its value.
Plan: use \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\), cancel the bigger factorial, then multiply and divide.
steps:
Given: \(n = 8\), \(r = 5\).
To find: \({}^{8}C_{5}\).
Method: \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\). It is the permutation \({}^{n}P_{r}\) divided by \(r!\), because each group of \(r\) things can be put in order in \(r!\) ways.

Cancel \(5!\) and calculate
\[= \dfrac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5!}{5! \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{6} = 56\]
Why: \(8! = 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5!\), so \(5!\) cancels; then \(3! = 6\) cancels the 6 on top.

Check with Pascal's rule
\[{}^{7}C_{5} + {}^{7}C_{4} = 21 + 35\]
\[= 56 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Pascal's rule \({}^{n}C_{r} + {}^{n}C_{r-1} = {}^{n+1}C_{r}\) (proved in Question 14) gives the same value from smaller combinations.

blocks.explanation:
\({}^{3}C_{3}\) is the number of ways to choose 3 things out of 3 different things when order does not matter.
We must find its value.
Plan: use \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\), cancel the bigger factorial, then multiply and divide.
steps:
Given: \(n = 3\), \(r = 3\).
To find: \({}^{3}C_{3}\).
Method: \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\). It is the permutation \({}^{n}P_{r}\) divided by \(r!\), because each group of \(r\) things can be put in order in \(r!\) ways.

Use \(0! = 1\)
\[= \dfrac{3!}{3! \cdot 1} = 1\]
Why: \(0! = 1\) by definition (Section 7.2). This is the corollary \({}^{n}C_{n} = 1\): there is only one way to choose all the things.

Check by listing
From \(\{A, B, C\}\) the only group of 3 is \(\{A, B, C\}\) itself: 1 group \(\checkmark\)
Why: Choosing all the things leaves no choice at all.

blocks.explanation:
\({}^{10}C_{7}\) is the number of ways to choose 7 things out of 10 different things when order does not matter.
We must find its value.
Plan: use \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\), cancel the bigger factorial, then multiply and divide.
steps:
Given: \(n = 10\), \(r = 7\).
To find: \({}^{10}C_{7}\).
Method: \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\). It is the permutation \({}^{n}P_{r}\) divided by \(r!\), because each group of \(r\) things can be put in order in \(r!\) ways.

Cancel \(7!\) and calculate
\[= \dfrac{10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7!}{7! \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{720}{6} = 120\]
Why: \(10! = 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7!\). Also \({}^{10}C_{7} = {}^{10}C_{3}\): choosing 7 to take is the same as choosing 3 to leave.

Check with Pascal's rule
\[{}^{9}C_{7} + {}^{9}C_{6} = 36 + 84\]
\[= 120 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Pascal's rule \({}^{n}C_{r} + {}^{n}C_{r-1} = {}^{n+1}C_{r}\) (proved in Question 14) gives the same value from smaller combinations.
